section_title: What danger remains after a remarkable rescue?

versions.label: BSB
paragraphs: 1 At that time Merodach-baladan son of Baladan king of Babylon sent letters and a gift to Hezekiah, for he had heard about Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. 2 And Hezekiah welcomed the envoys gladly and showed them what was in his treasure house—the silver, the gold, the spices, and the precious oil, as well as his entire armory—all that was found in his storehouses. There was nothing in his palace or in all his dominion that Hezekiah did not show them. 3 Then the prophet Isaiah went to King Hezekiah and asked, “Where did those men come from, and what did they say to you?” “They came to me from a distant land,” Hezekiah replied, “from Babylon.” 4 “What have they seen in your palace?” Isaiah asked. “They have seen everything in my palace,” answered Hezekiah. “There is nothing among my treasures that I did not show them.”

5 Then Isaiah said to Hezekiah, “Hear the word of the LORD of Hosts: 6 The time will surely come when everything in your palace and all that your fathers have stored up until this day will be carried off to Babylon. Nothing will be left, says the LORD. 7 And some of your descendants, your own flesh and blood, will be taken away to be eunuchs in the palace of the king of Babylon.” 8 But Hezekiah said to Isaiah, “The word of the LORD that you have spoken is good.” For he thought, “At least there will be peace and security in my lifetime.”

context_lines: The king of Babylon sends letters and a gift after hearing of Hezekiah’s illness and recovery. Hezekiah welcomes the envoys and shows them his treasures, supplies and armory. When Isaiah asks what they have seen, the king acknowledges that nothing has been withheld.

The Lord’s answer turns the display of wealth into a warning. Everything accumulated in the palace will one day be carried to Babylon, and some of Hezekiah’s descendants will serve there as eunuchs. The power sending a friendly gift is also the destination named in the coming loss.

Hezekiah calls the Lord’s word good, thinking of peace and security during his lifetime. The chapter closes with relief for the present generation alongside a grave warning about those to come. The earlier rescue from Assyria has not removed the need for faithful trust.
common_interpretation_lines: [Henry’s explanation of the parallel account](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/2_kings/20.htm) and [Gill](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/isaiah/39.htm) read the display as pride and confidence in human recognition. Henry connects it with an opportunity to speak of God’s work that was instead occupied by the king’s possessions. [Second Chronicles 32:24–31](https://biblehub.com/bsb/2_chronicles/32.htm) also links this period with pride, humbling and the test presented by the Babylonian envoys.

For Hezekiah’s final response, Henry, Gill and the [Cambridge commentary on verse 8](https://biblehub.com/commentaries/cambridge/isaiah/39.htm) read it as acceptance of God’s sentence and gratitude that mercy remains in its postponement. Gill explicitly argues that it need not mean indifference to his descendants.
The warning still stands in those readings. A period of peace in Hezekiah’s life does not reverse the announced loss of the palace’s treasures or the exile of his descendants.
god_plan_lines: The move toward Babylon becomes a major part of the history leading to Christ. [Matthew 1:11–17](https://biblehub.com/bsb/matthew/1.htm) marks the exile as a turning point in Jesus’ genealogy, then continues through the generations after it to Jesus, called Christ.

This is a connection in the unfolding biblical story, not a statement that Matthew directly quotes Isaiah 39. The exile is a real judgment and loss, yet it does not prevent God’s purpose from continuing through the family line.

Beside the Lord’s earlier promise concerning David, the ending leaves the reader looking beyond one king’s lifetime. Lasting hope rests in God’s faithfulness through judgment and restoration, ultimately reaching the promised Christ.
